title: Indian Mutual Funds Halt Bulk Gold ETF Subscriptions Ahead of Festive Season
excerpt: About 17 fund houses have closed new lump sums and SIP registrations in gold ETF fund-of-funds from October 15-16, while existing SIPs and redemptions continue.
body:
• About 17 Indian mutual fund houses, including HDFC, Kotak, ICICI Prudential, SBI and UTI, have suspended fresh subscriptions to gold ETF fund-of-funds from October 15-16, until further notice.
  • What you can and cannot do now: new lump sums, switch-ins and new SIP/STP registrations in these FoFs are stopped; SIPs registered before the cut-off continue, and redemptions and switch-outs remain open.
  • Gold ETF inflows jumped to Rs 4,450.61 crore in September 2026, up 71% from Rs 2,596.70 crore in August, according to AMFI data.
  • The fund notices gave no reason; Reuters reported the halt followed a nudge from SEBI, with the rupee under pressure and festive gold demand about to peak.

Several large Indian mutual fund houses have suspended bulk subscriptions to gold exchange-traded funds and the fund-of-funds that feed into them, just ahead of the festive season when gold buying traditionally peaks. According to Reuters, the notices were issued late on Thursday by houses including Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund, UTI Mutual Fund and HDFC Mutual Fund, and none cited a reason. A tally by Angel One put the number at about 17 fund houses, with restrictions taking effect on October 15 or 16.

What Exactly Has Stopped

The restrictions target the mutual fund route into gold, principally gold ETF fund-of-funds (FoFs) — schemes that invest in gold ETFs for investors who do not want to buy ETF units through a demat account — and some combined gold-silver passive FoFs. Across the houses, the pattern is consistent: fresh and additional lump-sum purchases are closed, switch-ins are blocked, and new SIP and STP registrations are not being accepted. Several houses, including ICICI Prudential, Tata, DSP and Invesco, have also stopped SIP and STP top-ups.

Existing investors are largely protected. SIPs and STPs registered before each house's cut-off continue to be processed at the applicable net asset value, and there is no restriction on redemptions, switch-outs or systematic withdrawal plans. None of the notices sets a reopening date; most describe the suspension as in force until further notice.

Why Now

The timing is the story. Indians celebrate Dussehra in October and Diwali in early November, when buying gold is considered auspicious, and demand was already running hot: inflows into gold ETFs reached Rs 4,450.61 crore in September, a 71% jump from Rs 2,596.70 crore in August, according to data from the Association of Mutual Funds in India cited by Angel One. Inflows into gold and silver ETFs also surged during last year's festive season, Reuters reported, as investors turned to precious metals amid lacklustre stock market returns.

The macroeconomic backdrop points the other way. The rupee has been under pressure this year from a surge in global oil prices, which inflated India's import bill, and heavy selling by foreign investors in Indian equities. India is the world's second-largest consumer of gold and relies on imports for most of its demand, so a festive surge in paper gold translates into physical imports that can widen the trade deficit. The government raised import duties on gold and silver earlier this year. A mutual fund executive told Reuters the halt followed a nudge from the Securities and Exchange Board of India, and two bullion industry officials confirmed discussions with the regulator; SEBI did not respond to a Reuters request for comment outside business hours.

"It looks more like a precautionary measure to avoid a surge in imports in October."

— Bullion dealer at a private bank supplying ETFs, to Reuters

The Counterpoint

The same dealer called the move surprising, because gold imports had already fallen to $1.8 billion in September from $2.3 billion in August, and imports over the past two months were sharply lower than a year earlier and had not contributed to the trade deficit. On that reading, the suspension is pre-emptive demand management aimed at October, not a response to an import surge already under way.

What Investors Can Do

Investors who already hold these FoFs need to do nothing: holdings are unaffected, running SIPs continue, and money can be redeemed at any time. Investors who wanted to start a new gold allocation through the mutual fund route this week cannot do so in the restricted schemes until subscriptions reopen. The notices do not restrict gold ETFs traded on exchanges, which are bought and sold through a demat account like shares. As with any festive-season purchase, the distinction that matters is the route, not the metal: the suspension closes one door, temporarily, and leaves the others open.
